title: US Budget Deficit Swells to $1.99 Trillion in Fiscal 2026, Largest in Five Years
excerpt: Record receipts of $5.40 trillion were outrun by record outlays of $7.40 trillion, as debt service hit $1.36 trillion, tariff refunds followed a Supreme Court ruling, and defence spending rose $48 billion.
body:
• The US budget deficit rose $217 billion to $1.99 trillion in fiscal 2026, up 12% from $1.78 trillion in fiscal 2025 and the largest shortfall since fiscal 2021.
  • Receipts were a record $5.40 trillion, up 3%; outlays were a record $7.40 trillion, up 6% — spending grew twice as fast as revenue.
  • Debt-service outlays hit a record $1.36 trillion, up 12%, as total US debt passed $40 trillion; defence spending rose $48 billion to $917 billion.
  • A Supreme Court ruling voiding much of the tariff programme triggered $145 billion of refunds, cutting net tariff income 11% to about $173 billion.

The US budget deficit widened to nearly $2 trillion in fiscal 2026, Treasury Department figures showed on Friday, as record tax receipts were outpaced by record spending — including the cost of servicing a national debt that has passed $40 trillion. The $1.99 trillion shortfall for the year ended September 30, the first full budget year of President Trump's second term, was up from $1.78 trillion in fiscal 2025 and is the third-largest annual deficit on record, behind only the pandemic years.

The arithmetic

The Congressional Budget Office estimated the same total: receipts of $5.403 trillion, up $169 billion or 3% on larger individual income and payroll tax collections, against outlays of $7.396 trillion, up $386 billion or 6%. Net interest was among the fastest-growing lines. Debt-service outlays reached a record $1.36 trillion, up $144 billion, a category now exceeded only by Social Security and the combined Medicare and Medicaid programmes.

Tariffs, refunds and defence

One driver was trade policy itself. A Supreme Court ruling this year negating a large portion of the tariffs imposed in the administration's first year triggered $145 billion of tariff refunds, and net tariff receipts fell $22 billion — an 11% decline to about $173 billion. Defence spending rose 6% to $917 billion, a $48 billion increase; a Treasury official said it was not clear how much of that rise was attributable to the war with Iran. Spending on Social Security, Medicare and other benefit programmes also grew.

"Careening toward an ominous fiscal crisis."

— Carolyn Bourdeaux, Concord Coalition, on the deficit path absent action by lawmakers

Why markets care

A deficit of this size, run by an economy that is neither at war on that scale nor in recession, has to be financed in the bond market every week. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield crossed 5% last month, its highest since the summer of 2007, which raises the government's own refinancing costs and feeds directly into mortgage and corporate borrowing rates. Fiscal watchdogs argue the mismatch is now structural: revenues set records and the gap still widened by an eighth in a single year.

What happens next

The CBO's longer view offers no automatic correction: on current trajectories, interest remains one of the largest items in the budget and debt held by the public climbs as a share of GDP. The political fight over the fiscal 2027 budget — and a debt-limit deadline expected by mid-2027 — will decide whether the $2 trillion year becomes the new baseline.
